sections.title: Woord Vooraf In Memoriam (p.2)
sections.text: FOREWORD In your hands, you have the annual report of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2021. In this report, you can read about the deployments the navy undertook during extensive international operations and exercises, as well as the actions taken by the shore organization to facilitate these deployments. The year began with COVID-19 measures, which caused many planned activities to be canceled. Nevertheless, the units managed to pick up the pace by creatively and responsibly resuming their work. Throughout the year, the measures were relaxed, allowing the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) to deploy more extensively. In a safe manner, personnel followed many new courses, training sessions, and participated in (international) exercises. This was done differently than usual, sometimes from home or at the workplace while maintaining a distance of one and a half meters. After the devastating earthquake in Haiti, part of the island lay in ruins, and there were significant shortages of basic necessities. Various units of the KM set course for the affected island to provide assistance and deliver supplies. Marines were deployed to ensure that aid could be distributed safely among the population. We hope that this Yearbook will once again prove to be a useful reference work. Editorial Team Annual Reports Royal Netherlands Navy Foreword Commander of the Naval Forces Vice Admiral R.P. Tas took command on September 9 from Vice Admiral R.A. Kramer.

sections.text: Organizational overviews years can take important steps towards both recovery and renewal of the organization. In 2021, in addition to the operational budget, the Defense Materiel Budget Fund (DMF) was used for the first time. The expenditures by CZSK were higher in 2021 than initially allocated at the beginning of the year. Compared to the draft budget, the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) achieved more in readiness. Within material expenditures, the military component spent more in 2021 than indicated in the draft budget. The draft budget included a contribution to, among others, the Defense Materiel Organization (DMO) for the procurement of ammunition. This contribution was financed through the reallocation of personnel expenditures. Also, in personnel expenditures, KM spent a net million more in 2021 than indicated in the draft budget. The cause was the additional expenditures for hiring. The hiring included not only temporary workers but also the hiring of operational management and IT consultants. Within the Navy, there was a shortfall in the personnel roster. The hiring was necessary to bring in essential personnel to prevent stagnation. During an exercise near Plymouth, a crew member of Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën fired a 12.7 mm machine gun.

P.F. Willemse The Directorate Personnel and Organization (DP&O) is the supporting directorate within the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) in the areas of personnel, training, healthcare, and organization. DP&O is the directorate that, within its scope and resources, ensures that the personnel of the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) have every opportunity to further develop and grow and adequately responds to those matters in the environment that can contribute to good employment practices. For 2021, the focal points of the directorate were: Restructuring towards future-proof training and individual instruction. This includes developments in the areas of simulation, the learning environment of the future, and studies related to the organizational structure of the Operational Command (OKM). Ensuring that inspiring vocational education takes place within CZSK by modernizing training through the use of modern learning tools, innovation, and establishing a connection between the operational and training domains. Restructuring training for flexible working, ensuring the social and physical safety of students and staff, and the practical application of Diversity & Inclusion (D&I). sections.text: Personnel and Organization The intensification of cooperation with industry and employment agencies as part of recruitment. Transition of P&O KM to a more sustainable personnel system in which personnel are more central. The development of a CZSK Policy Plan on Diversity & Inclusion. Further development of alignment between the CZSK training calendar and the Operational Year Plan (OJP). The disentanglement of the Bureau Flexible Capacity and the implementation of further professionalization of the Royal Netherlands Navy Reserve. Ensuring that we contribute sufficiently to the recruitment and retention of personnel according to a strategic communication plan. Legal Affairs (JUZA) Head: Commander (cdr) (LD) mr. E.P.J. Schelkers The JUZA department is part of the DP&O, one of the five line directorates of the CZSK. The department advises and supports CZSK, the directors of CZSK, and commanders of units on all legal issues that arise. JUZA provides legal advice and acts as a point of contact for the directors and commanders within the CZSK. Additionally, JUZA monitors the legal and administrative diligence of the operations within the CZSK. The main areas of law that the department deals with include (military) criminal and disciplinary law, operational law, and constitutional and administrative law. These areas of law are organized into three different bureaus. This allows every employee at JUZA to function as the first point of contact (counter function) for questions directed to the department. Therefore, JUZA does not provide legal advice to individual military personnel but does assist them if necessary. In criminal or disciplinary matters, JUZA is primarily involved on the side of CZSK and the Ministry of Defence as an organization. sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.4)
sections.text: The Personnel and Organization Directorate achieves this by providing personnel with the opportunity to develop and grow. In this way, P&O, as a career development organization, makes a relevant contribution to Defense and the labor market. By engaging and inspiring employees, the possibility for flexible deployment in the future is created, allowing room for (innovative) initiatives. Horstman EMSD The year was once again a year full of challenges for NLBEOPS, especially due to the pandemic. The school had already established a robust organization in 2020, which allowed the staff to quickly anticipate the frequent COVID-19 waves this year. The training was adjusted multiple times to the prevailing circumstances and medical challenges. Thanks to good logistical support, internal operations could be maintained. Through the prevailing measures and the consistent use of self-tests, the school significantly reduced the risk of internal infection. A combination of flu-like symptoms and COVID-19 still led to some peaks in temporary staff absence and the necessity to adjust micro-planning. Each department critically and pragmatically assessed operations in relation to teleworking/remote working and the healthy work/life balance. The personnel filling of NLBEOPS was approximately 85%. The largest personnel shortages were present in the VeVa department, at the Defense Navigation School (DVS), and Above Water Warfare. The personnel situation gradually improved at VeVa. An additional burden for NLBEOPS was the necessary assignment of personnel for deployments and support of the fleet. Also in 2021, the school had fewer interactions with external and foreign partners, resulting in a significant decrease in the number of visits and ceremonies this year. Nevertheless, it was possible to arrange some work visits and international forums at the school. The most important national visits were from the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), the Inspector General of the Armed Forces (IGK), the Commander of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (C-ZSK), and several directors of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command. Furthermore, there were visits and participation in training and forums at the school from NATO and European allies. The majority of ceremonial events were canceled or took place in a limited form. In terms of material readiness, quality declined. The main concerns involved the (again) postponed planning for the replacement of the Schooff, the water leakage and stormwater drainage at the DVS, the deteriorating condition of the trainer park at NLBEOPS and DVS, and the often sluggish and complex process of maintenance, repair, and replacement of equipment and trainers/simulators. More reports were made of defects and failures of trainers, which affected the smooth operation of the trainer runs.

sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2021_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-9 68 Operations Directorate After several weeks of maintenance and preparation, the ASD was successfully conducted just before the summer leave. During this, the ship also tested the SMART-ELR radar with various scenarios. The system was capable of simultaneously performing air defense and Ballistic Missile Defense (BMD). The ship also fired Evolved Sea Sparrow Missiles at two Banshee 80 drones. Additionally, it successfully executed an "enable Launch on Remote." Based on radar data from Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën, the USS Paul Ignatius was able to launch an SM-3 at a ballistic target even before the American ship had it visible on its own radar. This had not been demonstrated before and was a significant step for the Netherlands in the field of BMD. The ASD concluded with Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën launching a Harpoon near Andoya. After the summer leave, it continued the training trajectory with SARC-4 under the leadership of STC, combined with operating in a maritime task group led by Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën during the NOST off the coast of Britain.

In the past, various drones, particularly the PUMA, have been flown from ships of the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM). During Joint Warrior, the UAS Section worked closely with a team from the Recce Sniper Troop. The UAS operators collaborated with the Recce operators to explore how they could work together more effectively in gathering information. By deploying UAS operators alongside the Recce operator and utilizing the 'live-feed data' obtained, Recce operators can sometimes position themselves in a less vulnerable manner. Additionally, the UAS systems can generate images more easily, which Recce operators would otherwise have to work harder to obtain. This could include images behind buildings or highly zoomed-in images within a building to ascertain what is happening there. Joint Warrior was an educational exercise and contributed to further experience building regarding the deployment of UAS in the maritime and amphibious domain and a first collaboration between UAS and Recce operators. Twelve new operators for NLMARSOF In recent weeks, the T-Squadron of NLMARSOF trained in Curaçao. This exercise was the final exercise of the NLMARSOF training 2020-2021. It encompassed nearly all aspects of SOF work, and the aspiring operators faced various challenging scenarios. With the completion of the final exercise, the twelve newly qualified operators concluded a grueling year. A year in which they were prepared to join the operational squadrons of NLMARSOF. Working within the operational squadrons, they can be deployed in various SOF operations. SOF Genie ADV Breaching training In August and September, NLMARSOF independently conducted the SOF Gn ADV Breaching training for the first time. The group of trainees included operators from both M-Squadron and C-Squadron. Instructors from NLMARSOF provided the training in collaboration with external partners from the Engineering Training and Education Center in Reek and the United States. Evacuation Afghanistan On Monday afternoon, August 16, the operators of the Non-Foreseeable Special Operation section of C-Squadron were ordered to cut short their summer leave and report as soon as possible to the Nieuwe Haven in Den Helder. There, the entire equipment of the unit was packed and ready for action abroad. Upon arrival at the marsofterrein there, the marines learned that they would fly to Kabul together with two KCT teams and a BSB team to assist in the evacuation of Dutch citizens and status holders. Once landed at Kabul airport, the operators found themselves in a chaotic situation. Within the Dutch task unit, the NLMARSOF section was responsible for securing the flights between Kabul and Islamabad. Ultimately, the task unit facilitated approximately 2,500 people to safety via 21 Dutch evacuation flights, including more than thirty interpreters and their families. With the last C-130 flight to Islamabad on August 26, nearly twenty years of Dutch military presence in Afghanistan came to an end. NLMARSOF operators contributed to this since the first deployment of Taskgroup Orange in 2005.

At the Dutch initiative, the second Assembly indicated to the Council for the period 2020-2023 the theme “the effective implementation of the Revised Strategic Plan keeping in mind to apply the principles of ISO9001.” The fifth Council then decided that “ISO9001 principles will be experimented on the development of the Product Specification for ENCs, S-101 ed. 2.0.0.” The first steps for S-100 implementation at HYD have now been taken, with the production of test datasets for three different standards. This resulted in Zr.Ms. Urania fully fulfilling its primary task of practical education for cadets, just as in 2020. In addition, the ship undertook tasks that it had not performed before. An example of such a new task took place immediately after the annual maintenance period in the winter. For three weeks, Zr.Ms. Urania undertook a voyage with participants from the Post Active Network Royal Netherlands Navy. This network provides support to post-active naval colleagues in processing traumatic events they experienced during their careers. This was an impressive and successful voyage during which Zr.Ms. Urania created the conditions for the participants to openly share these experiences, thus contributing to the care for former colleagues. After the necessary quarantine period, the ship shifted its focus back to the education of cadets in May and June. Even during this period, more was possible than in 2020, but due to limited international travel options for crew changes, only Dutch and Belgian ports were visited. Unlike regular years, July was a quiet month. However, in August it became possible to participate in the first maritime events after COVID-19. Zr.Ms. Urania participated with an ad-hoc crew from Defensity College in Hanse Sail in Rostock and Sail Bremerhaven. In addition to displaying flags at these events, Zr.Ms. Urania also contributed to increasing job satisfaction by providing Defense colleagues the opportunity to sail along. In September, it was again possible to conduct VIP sailing days on the IJsselmeer. In October, the sailing season concluded with an educational week for a group of cadets who had previously been unable to participate due to an infection. Subsequently, Zr.Ms. Urania took part in the Race of the Classics with a crew composed of the Young Defense network.

Borsje-Senders Mission The mission of CZMCARIB is derived from the mission of CZSK and translates to the environment in the West as follows: 'Providing security in the Caribbean.' This one sentence encapsulates what CZMCARIB stands for and focuses at the strategic level on the realization of the three main tasks of defense in the Caribbean: Protecting the integrity and interests of the territory of Curaçao, Aruba, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB is responsible for the territorial integrity of the Caribbean countries of the Kingdom and Caribbean Netherlands. The own and visiting operational units have a so-called threshold function. This means that through our presence and our activities, we have a deterrent effect against potential hostilities from foreign countries or organizations. Promoting the international rule of law and stability. The second main task also includes the deployment for international law enforcement, such as combating the smuggling of weapons and

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.3)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean is focused on countering drug trafficking by sea. CZMCARIB promotes regional security and stability by, among other things, conducting counter illicit trafficking operations and through international military cooperation. The United States and France are the main international partners in this effort. C-ZMCARIB fulfills the CIT task as Commander Task Group 4.4 (CTG 4.4), a subordinate commander of the American Joint Interagency Task Force South. The support of civil authorities is also a priority. The Dutch Armed Forces have developed into a structural security partner within the Kingdom. With its highly developed specialist and unique capabilities, the armed forces now offer broader support options. CZMCARIB provides units that can be deployed for military assistance to Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB also provides support to third parties, primarily to the Coast Guard in the Caribbean (KWCARIB). C-ZMCARIB is also the Director of KWCARIB. It also provides emergency assistance during disasters and crises. Finally, CZMCARIB supports the Social Development Programs in Curaçao and Aruba. Zr.Ms. Holland and a FRISC were deployed off the coast of Haiti.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.4)
sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Area Vision In order to realize the mission of CZMCARIB as adequately as possible in light of the surrounding changes, a vision has been established. The vision of CZMCARIB is: ‘CZMCARIB is the relevant maritime and security partner in the Caribbean, as part of the CZSK’. This means that CZMCARIB aims to be recognized as the obvious and reliable partner when it comes to contributing to security in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom. ‘Relevant maritime’ and ‘security partner’ in the above vision refers to the fact that CZMCARIB assigns a high priority to the second and third core tasks. Due to national and international agreements, it wants to promote the international and local rule of law with its own resources, for example by contributing capabilities to (inter)national organizations or by providing military assistance. With these own resources, it can be deployed for many diverse scenarios to support civil authorities, for example for conducting searches, tracking, diving units, observation, and emergency assistance. CZMCARIB does this in good cooperation with national and international partners in the security chain. Reflection on 2021 Just like in 2020, COVID-19 also dominated this year. The pandemic had a significant impact on the operations of CZMCARIB as well as its operational activities. Local authorities, particularly from Curaçao, regularly called upon military assistance to support them with COVID-19 related activities. International Drug Enforcement In addition to the external defense of six islands of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, the Defense plays an important role in maintaining the international rule of law in the Caribbean area. Given the location of the islands, this primarily involves combating international drug trafficking by sea. The Navy in the Caribbean is thus closely integrated into the international drug enforcement organization Joint Interagency Task Force South based in Key West. The Commander (kltz) of the Navy in the Caribbean is therefore the commander of Task Group 4.4, one of the task groups of this organization.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.5)
sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean The task assigned to CZMCARIB from the Land Packages is to professionalize the Caribbean military, including modernizing the legal position and (re)establishing the Social Development Program for disadvantaged youth in both Aruba and Curaçao. Throughout the year, the department began drafting the CZMCARIB Ambition Document. This document looks ten years ahead and describes both the ambition in terms of personnel and equipment. The goal is to complete the Ambition Document in 2022 and formally present it to C-ZSK. Despite COVID-19, CMCARIB made a strong effort to expand the CARIB training hub. For example, work was done on a Forward Operating Base at the Wacawa training area in Curaçao and on a training village for Urban Operations at the Marine Barracks Savaneta in Aruba. In 2021, CZMCARIB took the first steps to pay extra attention to real estate in the area. The state of maintenance is insufficient, office spaces and barracks often do not meet standards, and various installations are no longer maintainable, including air handling systems. Relief goods are being unloaded in Haiti.

In addition to the frequent deployment for primary task three, CZMCARIB made a significant contribution to primary task two this year by conducting Counter Illicit Trafficking operations and providing emergency assistance in the Caribbean. Station Ship Caribbean (SSCG) In 2021, there was one ship with two different crews designated as SSCG under the command of C-ZMCARIB. Due to unforeseen defects and repairs to Zr.Ms. Groningen, CZMCARIB did not have an SSCG available during the first period until Zr.Ms. Holland arrived in the West at the end of May. The SSCG was equipped with an NH90 onboard helicopter. In addition to the usual deployment for KWCARIB and CTG 4.4, the SSCG contributed to emergency assistance in Haiti. This was in response to the severe earthquake that struck the country on August 14. From August 19 to September 2, the SSCG distributed, among other things, 35,000 liters of water and 25,000 kg of goods in the hard-to-reach affected areas for Netherlands Task Force Haiti. The Task Force consisted of the MHKC, SSCG, Marine Squadron CARIB (MSC), the Boat Platoon, Company in the West (CIDW), and EGB.

In collaboration with international units, approximately 10,200 kg and 1,900 kg of contraband were removed from the trade market in 2021 by CTG 4.4 and KWCARIB, respectively, through confiscation. These international operations were carried out by the ship with various countries such as the United States, France, Colombia, and the United Kingdom. From May 26 to June 5, rehearsals were conducted in the Windward Islands for the hurricane season, which runs from June 1 to November 30. During the exercise, MHKC worked closely with local authorities and aid organizations to ensure smooth cooperation during the hurricane season. In 2021, the Control Department of CZMCARIB worked to support C-ZMCARIB in the preparation, execution, progress, and quality of financial policy advice. It also compiled the budget, established the spending program, and provided management and steering reports. 

Finance: In 2021, CZSK made budget cuts in several areas. In this process, less budget was allocated to the Caribbean than was originally available. CZMCARIB had a budget of 18.7 million euros in 2021. Due to limited travel opportunities caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the fact that fewer external units conducted exercises in the Caribbean, fewer activities took place. CZMBARIB also organized fewer activities for its own units due to the pandemic. As a result, most foreign exercises were canceled, and units traveled much less between the islands for training. The realization of the budget fell short as a result. Furthermore, the establishment of the Country Package led to a 12.5% reduction in the salaries of local staff. The Social Development Programs were not executed, and the additional personnel capacity within the development of Caribbean Military Personnel (CARMIL) was not filled immediately. Because CZMCARIB paid the currency claim of 1.9 million euros itself, the full budget was realized in 2021.

Management Information: In 2021, CZMCARIB reported on the year 2020 based on a plan-do-check-act cycle and prepared the annual plan for 2022. With this annual plan, they looked not only at the short term but also at the long term to be able to plan in a timely manner. In further improving operations, the focus was on enhancing the quality of input and securing the changed operations, with the motto 'strong together.'

sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean initiated the transport of CIDW to Aruba and MSC to Curaçao in January. Due to the risk of COVID-19 infections and the complexity of testing, it was decided not to conduct a rest and recreation port visit. In March, the annual maintenance began, during which the crew prepared the ship for the hurricane season. This process was hampered by a strict lockdown in Curaçao, requiring personnel to work from home or take leave. Fortunately, the overall impact remained small, except for a few specialists from DMI who could not come. In Sint Maarten, the ship made use of Zr.Ms. Pelikaan in Curaçao.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.16)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean provided the crew with the opportunity to train in the main deployment: transporting large quantities of cargo, conducting hydrographic surveys of the port, logistically facilitating colleagues stationed on land (in accordance with the shit, shave and shower routine), and supplying water and fuel. Additionally, a reconnaissance was conducted for the new crew members on Sint Maarten, focusing on locations that play an important role during deployments (airport, hospital, headquarters, etc.). With the completion of HUREX, Zr.Ms. Pelikaan was ready for deployment with a notice to move of 48 hours, allowing the ship to arrive in the disaster area within hours after the passage of a hurricane. After HUREX, the ship collaborated for several days with the boat platoon in Curaçao, providing amphibious support to T-squadron, a training unit of NLMARSOF. In June, internal preparations were again made, and a port visit to Aruba was conducted as part of rest and recreation. After a five-week leave, the crew worked under the leadership of MOST during a two-week CT. Due to COVID-19, the leadership decided not to conduct a port visit due to the significant impact a potential infection could have on the training program. In September, the ship participated in the annual exercise Windward Express, where it executed a training program on Sint Maarten for two troops from the MSC of Aruba. The focus of the exercise was on amphibious operations and optimizing cooperation between Zr.Ms. Pelikaan and the MSC. In October, the ship supported the DDG, where the very shallow water team received logistical assistance on the west coast of Aruba and the deep dive team in Caracas Bay in Curaçao. Due to an incoming request, the ship was able to provide support on relatively short notice in November for renewing military cooperation with Suriname surrounding the Surinamese independence celebration. For this purpose, two Surinamese officers flew to Curaçao for a four-week military exchange. Zr.Ms. Pelikaan, with the embarked boat platoon from Aruba, also made a port visit in Paramaribo. During this period, there was intensive contact with the Surinamese armed forces, authorities, and population. For instance, there was an exchange in the 24 hours prior to the port visit, the ship conducted a riverine training with the Surinamese navy, provided numerous tours and lessons on board, and facilitated a reception with the Dutch embassy for, among others, the

sections.text: 7_KM_Annual_Report_2021_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-19 138 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Region Social Work Service (DBMW) Regional Team Leader: Lieutenant (ltz1) H.J.H. Goetzee The main tasks that BMW performs in the Caribbean region are assistance, service provision, reporting, support after traumatic events, and crisis intervention. For the CARIB region, the service, together with the Chaplaincy Service and in Aruba also with P&O, is responsible for notifying family announcements. They are available on a 24/7 basis for personnel and their families. This was the second year in which COVID-19 played a restrictive role, but the situation normalized during 2021, allowing for more regular opportunities to carry out the work. For instance, the service resumed work visits to Bonaire, where the KMar is active, and to Sint Maarten to be more accessible to personnel and their families on these islands. After the emergency aid to Haiti, the department provided aftercare for the units that were deployed. In addition to the regular BMW support for employees and their families, activities for post-active veterans resumed in 2021. In Curaçao, the Veterans Association Curaçao was active and represents the interests of veterans residing on the island. BMW was in contact with this association to provide access for veterans living in Curaçao and Aruba from the position as a partner within the National Care System for Veterans. On both islands, various assistance contacts with post-active veterans were established. As part of veteran care, the service also maintained contact with the Veterans Care Desk of the General Civil Pension Fund in the Netherlands. Medical Service CZMCARIB Head: Captain (ktz) R.J. Joosten The Primary Health Care Company (EGB) and the Defense Dental Service provide primary care in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom from the Health Center Curaçao. Additionally, there is a branch at the location in Aruba. At both centers, they provide integrated care to military personnel and deployed Dutch civilian employees. The Dental Service and EGB in the CARIB also provide 24/7 care to the accompanying family members of the deployed employees. Furthermore, the staff of the EGB provides operational support to the MHKC.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.20)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean in 2021 was also dominated by the concerns of the pandemic. The EGB provided personnel to the local GGD after a previous support request to assist in GGD COVID-19 testing sites, conducting contact tracing among its own ranks, and opening its own testing site at MBPAR. The organization also provided daily care for positively tested personnel who were placed in quarantine at MKSUF. This continued throughout the year. In addition to this care, a vaccination program was initiated in Curaçao by the local GGD. On April 1, they requested EGB to assist them by opening a site at MBPAR to administer vaccinations to military personnel and their family members, as well as to civil servants in crucial professions from the country and kingdom. On April 4, EGB military personnel vaccinated at MBPAR, and the medical teams from CIDW and a local nurse from the Curaçao militia also administered shots. On the opening day, they provided vaccinations to over 1,000 people (well above the numbers at other vaccination sites on the island). Therefore, this continued for another two and a half weeks at the base. After this period, this site was closed, and EGB supported other vaccination centers in the country with personnel. In addition to all pandemic-related care, the service supported military training and exercises that continued throughout the year. Vaccination of military personnel.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.23)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean lasted nearly a year and a half and concluded as planned after the completion of the initial training of the Coast Guard in 2021. The maritime support points are not yet at full strength and can currently only be deployed '16/7', but the transition to '24/7' availability of the maritime support points will be gradually achieved with the implementation of the Long-Term Plan in the coming years. Equipment 2021 was an important year for, among other things, the project 'improving shore radar detection' of the Coast Guard, aimed at contributing to the operation's direction based on information. During the year, most of the fixed shore radar chain was replaced. Six of the eight locations spread across the Leeward Islands have been equipped with new masts containing new radars and protective housings. The remaining two locations will be replaced in early 2022, after which the entire chain will be tested. With this replacement process, the Coast Guard is making a significant leap in its imaging capabilities around the Leeward Islands and will reduce maintenance costs. Bonaire The collaboration with the chain partners led to the establishment of the Multidisciplinary Maritime Hub Bonaire. In 2021, all involved services signed a letter of intent. Coast Guard Netherlands Director: Captain (ktz) J. van Zanten For the second consecutive year, Covid-19 had a significant impact on society and on the Coast Guard. Despite repeatedly scaling up and down restrictive measures in 2021, the Coast Guard carried out its regular tasks in the areas of service, enforcement, and maritime security. The service operated with the knowledge that the Netherlands has only one Maritime Communication and Coordination Center (CCC) for the execution of its tasks, which coordinates the deployment of aircraft, helicopters, and units from partner KNRM. Throughout the year, the service conducted additional Baksgwijse inspections of the cadets during the final exercise on Texel.

sections.title: Bijlagen Colofon 19 12 2022 (p.4)
sections.text: Appendices measures to ensure the continuity of SAR operations. The way in which the partners collaborated with the Coast Guard to carry out their tasks as effectively as possible despite these measures proved to be a reliable and stable factor in 2021. The flexibility of personnel and resources was crucial in this regard. The task of maritime security is taking more shape within the Coast Guard, and starting this year, a separate chapter has been dedicated to the implementation of this new, third main task in the Annual Report. For the proper execution of particularly pre-arrival analyses, the right resources were not yet made available to the Coast Guard in 2021. In addition to regular Coast Guard tasks, a Coast Guard aircraft was deployed during two periods in the context of EU-Frontex in the Mediterranean Sea, as well as during the flooding in Limburg. The aircraft of the Coast Guard flew a record number of flight hours in 2021, and the agreements regarding the deployment of SAR helicopters have been improved. Due to the withdrawal of vessels from the Rijksrederij of more than twenty percent, the deployment of these vessels at sea fell short of the assignment from the Combined Annual Plan. The renewal and modernization of the Coast Guard is taking more shape. Not only has progress been made in the ICT part of the Maritime Operations Center project, but in 2021, the architect and project management were selected for the new construction, an important step towards the realization of the new operations center. Intensive work has been done with the commissioning parties of the Coast Guard and the Rijksrederij to find a solution for the implementation of the 24/7 enforcement concept with the existing vessels. An important development in the tasks of the Coast Guard is the intensification of tasks to ensure shipping safety in the context of offshore wind energy. The ongoing construction of wind farms in the North Sea requires additional monitoring of shipping. To this end, an extra desk has been set up at the CCC, additional personnel have been recruited, and since 2021, one additional Emergency Recovery & Towing Vessel has been patrolling in the southern North Sea. For the influx of personnel, a limited reorganization process was completed in 2021. Progress has been made in the development of the internal organization of the Coast Guard due to the influx of new personnel in previous years, both in operational and supporting processes. This is particularly visible in the crisis organization, structuring functional ICT management, implementing GDPR legislation, documenting processes, and renewing operational agreements with partner services.
